dx: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis with calcium phosphate stones in Sjogren syndrome
case: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of two episodes of left flank pain over the past year and increasing muscle weakness. She has had dry eyes and a dry mouth for 3 years. Serum anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are positive. Serum studies show sodium 139 mEq/L (136 to 145), potassium 2.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), chloride 114 mEq/L (98 to 106), and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (22 to 28). Arterial pH is 7.30 (7.35 to 7.45). Urine pH is 6.5, and urine culture shows no growth. CT scan shows bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis and a 6-mm stone in the left renal pelvis. Analysis of a previously passed stone shows calcium phosphate. Diagnosis: distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis due to Sjogren syndrome, with calcium phosphate stones.

questions.stem: Her hypokalemia results largely from increased potassium secretion by principal cells of the cortical collecting duct, enhanced by aldosterone released in response to mild volume depletion. Which of the following most directly drives this potassium secretion?
options: Apical potassium reabsorption by H+/K+-ATPase
Lumen-negative voltage from sodium entry through ENaC
Paracellular potassium flux driven by a lumen-positive voltage
Aquaporin-2 insertion that concentrates luminal potassium
approach: Locate the cell: principal cells of the cortical collecting duct secrete potassium.
Recall what aldosterone does there: more ENaC channels in the apical membrane and more Na+/K+-ATPase in the basolateral membrane.
Link the two: sodium entering through ENaC makes the lumen negative, which pulls potassium out of the cell through apical K+ channels.
questions.why: Aldosterone binds a cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells and increases apical ENaC channels and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. Sodium moves into the cell through ENaC without an accompanying anion, so the lumen becomes electrically negative. The pump keeps intracellular potassium high, and the negative lumen pulls potassium out through apical ROMK channels. In distal RTA, failed H+ secretion and volume-driven aldosterone both increase this potassium loss.
whyNot: The H+/K+-ATPase sits in alpha-intercalated cells and reabsorbs potassium. It works against potassium loss and becomes important in potassium depletion.
Correct.
A lumen-positive voltage exists in the thick ascending limb and drives paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption. It does not drive potassium secretion in the collecting duct.
ADH inserts aquaporin-2 to reabsorb water. Water reabsorption does not create the electrical gradient that drives potassium secretion.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of her urine most directly accounts for the composition of her stones?
options: Acidic pH with high urate excretion
Alkaline pH from urease-producing bacteria
Acidic pH with high cystine excretion
Alkaline pH with low citrate excretion
approach: Note the stone type: calcium phosphate.
Recall that calcium phosphate precipitates in alkaline urine, and that citrate normally binds calcium and keeps it in solution.
Apply to distal RTA: the urine stays alkaline, and chronic acidosis increases proximal citrate reabsorption, so urinary citrate falls.
questions.why: Calcium phosphate is much less soluble in alkaline urine. In distal RTA the collecting duct cannot secrete H+, so urine pH stays above 5.5 even during acidemia. Chronic acidosis also increases proximal tubule reabsorption of citrate, so little citrate is left to chelate urinary calcium, and acidosis releases calcium from bone, adding hypercalciuria. Together these drive calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis.
whyNot: Acidic urine with high urate favors uric acid stones, which are radiolucent and seen in gout and tumor lysis.
Urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus alkalinize urine and form struvite stones. Her urine culture is sterile, and her stones are calcium phosphate.
Cystine stones form in cystinuria, an inherited transport defect, and are more likely in acidic urine. They show hexagonal crystals.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient most reliably distinguishes her disorder from proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis?
options: Urine pH 6.5 with arterial pH 7.30
Serum potassium concentration of 2.9 mEq/L
Calculated serum anion gap of 10 mEq/L
Serum chloride concentration of 114 mEq/L
approach: List what types 1 and 2 share: normal anion gap, hyperchloremia, and hypokalemia.
Find the feature that differs: the ability to acidify urine when serum bicarbonate is low.
In proximal RTA, once serum bicarbonate falls below the lowered threshold, the intact distal nephron acidifies urine below 5.5. In distal RTA it cannot.
questions.why: Both proximal and distal RTA cause a normal anion gap, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia. In proximal RTA, the proximal tubule wastes bicarbonate until serum bicarbonate drops to a new, lower threshold, and then the healthy distal nephron can lower urine pH below 5.5. In distal RTA, alpha-intercalated cells cannot secrete H+, so the urine stays above 5.5 despite acidemia. A urine pH of 6.5 with an arterial pH of 7.30 therefore points to the distal type.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypokalemia occurs in both type 1 and type 2 RTA. It separates them from type 4, which causes hyperkalemia.
A normal anion gap is shared by all types of RTA. It separates RTA from ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis, not one RTA from another.
Hyperchloremia accompanies any normal anion gap acidosis, so it is present in both proximal and distal RTA.

questions.stem: Eight months later, she has severe left flank pain. CT shows a 5-mm stone impacted in the left ureter at the point where the ureter enters the true pelvis. Which of the following structures lies immediately posterior to the ureter at this site?
options: Psoas major muscle at the level of the L3 vertebra
Gonadal artery and vein in the abdomen
Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
Uterine artery lateral to the cervix
approach: Identify the site: where the ureter enters the true pelvis is the pelvic brim.
Trace the ureter: it descends on the psoas, then crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim.
This crossing is one of the three narrow points where stones lodge.
questions.why: The ureter runs down on the psoas major in the abdomen, then crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (the start of the external iliac artery) as it enters the pelvis. The ureter narrows at three points: the ureteropelvic junction, this crossing at the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction. Stones commonly lodge at each of them.
whyNot: The psoas lies behind the ureter in its abdominal course, above the pelvic brim. A stone stuck on the psoas would be in the mid ureter.
The gonadal vessels cross anterior to the ureter in the abdomen, not behind it, and they do this above the pelvic brim.
Correct.
The uterine artery crosses above and in front of the distal ureter near the cervix, deep in the pelvis. That site is at risk during hysterectomy.

dx: Calcium oxalate ureteral stone with renal colic
case: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe right flank pain that comes in waves and spreads into the right groin and scrotum. He has vomited twice and cannot find a comfortable position. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Testicular examination is normal. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 20 to 30 RBCs/hpf, and is negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm radiopaque stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild right hydronephrosis. Diagnosis: calcium oxalate ureteral stone with renal colic.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his pain is felt in the groin?
options: Irritation of the obturator nerve on the lateral pelvic wall
Stretch of parietal peritoneum innervated by the phrenic nerve
Shared T11 to L2 segments of ureteral and groin afferents
Sacral parasympathetic afferents from the bladder trigone
approach: Recognize the pain as visceral: it is colicky, poorly localized, and comes from stretch of the ureter and pelvis.
Recall that ureteral visceral afferents enter the cord at lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments, about T11 to L2.
Apply referred pain: the brain assigns the pain to skin supplied by the same segments, including the groin and scrotum (L1).
questions.why: Pain from a distended ureter travels in visceral afferent fibers that run with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at about T11 to L2. Somatic afferents from the flank, groin, and anterior scrotum enter those same segments. Because the signals converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, the brain reads the pain as coming from that skin. As the stone moves down the ureter, the pain tends to shift from the flank toward the groin.
whyNot: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh. Irritation by a pelvic mass or hernia causes medial thigh pain, not flank to groin colic.
The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) carries pain from diaphragmatic peritoneum to the shoulder, as in splenic rupture. It plays no part in ureteral pain.
Correct.
Afferents from the bladder trigone and neck run with pelvic splanchnic nerves to S2 to S4 and refer pain to the perineum and tip of the penis.

questions.stem: Six weeks later, metabolic evaluation shows serum calcium 11.1 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.2), serum phosphorus 2.2 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), an elevated serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration, and a 24-hour urine calcium of 360 mg (under 300). Which of the following most directly explains his increased intestinal calcium absorption?
options: PTH-induced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity
PTH-stimulated 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D in the liver
Increased renal 24-hydroxylation of calcitriol
Calcitonin-stimulated calcium uptake in the duodenum
approach: Read the pattern: high calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism.
Recall that PTH and low phosphate both stimulate 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule.
Follow the result: more calcitriol increases calcium absorption in the gut, which raises the filtered calcium load and the urine calcium.
questions.why: In primary hyperparathyroidism, PTH acts on the proximal tubule to increase 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which turns 25-hydroxyvitamin D into 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). The low serum phosphate, caused by PTH blocking proximal phosphate reabsorption, also stimulates this enzyme. Calcitriol raises intestinal calcium absorption. PTH increases distal calcium reabsorption, but the filtered calcium load rises so much that urine calcium still goes up, which promotes calcium stones.
whyNot: Correct.
Hepatic 25-hydroxylation is not under tight hormonal control. It depends mainly on the supply of vitamin D.
24-hydroxylation inactivates vitamin D and is favored when PTH is low and calcitriol is high. PTH suppresses it.
Calcitonin lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts. It does not drive intestinal calcium absorption.

topics: Vitamin D activation in the kidney

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of features is most consistent with the stone recovered from this patient?
options: Radiolucent stone with rhomboid or rosette crystals
Faintly opaque stone with hexagonal crystals
Radiopaque stone with coffin-lid prism crystals
Radiopaque stone with envelope-shaped crystals
approach: Start from the stone type: calcium oxalate, the most common stone.
Recall its features: calcium makes it radiopaque, and the dihydrate crystals look like envelopes (bipyramids).
Match each other option to its stone: rhomboid for uric acid, hexagonal for cystine, coffin-lid for struvite.
questions.why: Calcium oxalate makes up most kidney stones, and hypercalciuria is the usual underlying cause. Calcium-containing stones are radiopaque on plain films and CT. Calcium oxalate dihydrate crystals look like envelopes, and the monohydrate form looks like dumbbells. The appearance of crystals and stones lets you predict composition before formal analysis.
whyNot: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain films and show rhomboid or rosette crystals. They form in acidic urine, as in gout.
Cystine stones are faintly opaque and show flat hexagonal crystals. They come from inherited cystinuria.
Struvite stones are radiopaque and show coffin-lid crystals, but they form in alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria.
Correct.

questions.stem: Thirty-six hours later, the stone has not passed. He develops rigors, temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Repeat CT shows the stone still at the right ureterovesical junction with worsening right hydronephrosis. Which of the following most likely explains his deterioration?
options: Ascending infection limited to the bladder mucosa
Infection of stagnant urine above the obstructing stone
Hematogenous seeding of the renal cortex from skin flora
Intraperitoneal urine leak from rupture of the bladder dome
approach: Note the combination: fever and hypotension in a patient with a stone that still blocks the ureter.
Recall that urine trapped above an obstruction is not flushed out, so bacteria multiply there.
Conclude that he has an infected obstructed kidney (obstructive pyelonephritis) with sepsis, a complication that needs urgent drainage.
questions.why: Stones cause harm mainly by obstruction. Urine above the stone stagnates, the pelvis and calyces dilate, and bacteria that reach this static urine multiply without being washed out. An infected, obstructed kidney can progress quickly to pyonephrosis and urosepsis with fever and hypotension. Other complications of calculi include hydronephrosis, loss of renal function with long obstruction, and hematuria.
whyNot: Cystitis alone causes dysuria and frequency without high fever, rigors, or hypotension. It also would not explain worsening hydronephrosis.
Correct.
Hematogenous spread, often from Staphylococcus aureus, causes renal abscesses. It is much less common than ascending infection and does not follow from his obstruction.
Dome rupture follows blunt trauma to a full bladder and causes urinary ascites. Nothing in his course suggests bladder injury.

case: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of left flank pain for 2 days. She has passed kidney stones four times since the age of 9 years. Her 20-year-old brother also has recurrent stones, and her parents have never had stones. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urinalysis shows urine pH 5.5, 2+ blood, and flat hexagonal crystals. Urine glucose is negative. The urine cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. CT scan shows an 8-mm stone in the left renal pelvis and a 4-mm stone in the proximal left ureter, both faintly opaque. Diagnosis: cystinuria with recurrent cystine stones.

questions.stem: Pain from her proximal ureteral stone is carried by visceral afferent fibers. Which of the following nerves do these fibers travel with to reach the central nervous system?
options: Lumbar and lower thoracic splanchnic nerves
Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4
Vagal fibers passing through the celiac plexus
Subcostal and iliohypogastric nerves
approach: Classify the pain: ureteral distension is visceral pain.
Recall the rule: visceral pain from organs above the pelvic pain line travels back with sympathetic fibers.
Apply it to the ureter: the fibers run back through the lower thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves and enter the cord at about T11 to L2.
questions.why: Visceral pain fibers from the kidney and the abdominal ureter run backward along the sympathetic nerves (the lesser and least splanchnic and lumbar splanchnic nerves). They reach the spinal cord through the dorsal roots of about T11 to L2. This explains why the pain is felt in the flank, lower abdomen, and groin. Pelvic organs below the peritoneum send pain mainly with parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves instead.
whyNot: Correct.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry visceral pain from organs below the pelvic pain line, such as the bladder neck and cervix. The proximal ureter lies far above that level.
Vagal afferents carry physiological signals such as stretch and chemoreception. They do not carry pain from the ureter.
The subcostal and iliohypogastric nerves carry somatic sensation from the skin and muscles of the flank and lower abdominal wall. Ureteral distension is visceral pain.

questions.stem: On CT, her 4-mm proximal ureteral stone lies below the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter descends on the psoas major. Which of the following structures crosses directly anterior to the left ureter in this segment?
options: Genitofemoral nerve on the psoas major
Left renal vein anterior to the aorta
Left gonadal artery and vein
Lumbar sympathetic trunk on the vertebral bodies
approach: Place the stone: the abdominal ureter, descending on the psoas major.
Recall the ureter's relations there: muscle and nerve behind, gonadal vessels crossing in front.
Pick the structure that crosses anterior to it.
questions.why: In the abdomen the ureter runs down on the psoas major, with the genitofemoral nerve behind it on the muscle. The gonadal vessels run obliquely downward and cross anterior to the ureter in this segment. Lower down, the ureter crosses the common iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim and then runs along the pelvic wall to the bladder. Knowing these relations helps you read CT and understand surgical risk to the ureter.
whyNot: The genitofemoral nerve lies on the anterior surface of the psoas, behind the ureter.
The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava. It lies above and medial to the abdominal ureter.
Correct.
The lumbar sympathetic trunk lies along the vertebral bodies, posterior and medial to the ureter.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, which of the following best describes how the nephron normally handles the filtered cystine and dibasic amino acids that are lost in this patient's urine?
options: About two thirds reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
Nearly all reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
Nearly all reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb
About two thirds reabsorbed in the collecting duct
approach: Recall the segment: amino acids, like glucose, are reclaimed in the proximal tubule.
Separate the fractions: about two thirds applies to sodium and water, while nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed.
Link to the case: a missing proximal transporter lets cystine reach the urine in large amounts.
questions.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered sodium and water and nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids. Amino acids enter the cell through specific apical transporters, many of them sodium-coupled. In cystinuria, the transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine is defective, so these amino acids escape into the urine. Cystine is poorly soluble and forms stones.
whyNot: About two thirds is the fraction for sodium and water in the proximal tubule. Amino acid reabsorption there is nearly complete.
Correct.
The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- through Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransport and Mg2+ and Ca2+ by the paracellular route. It does not reclaim amino acids.
The collecting duct fine-tunes sodium, potassium, acid, and water. Amino acids are reabsorbed well before they reach it.

questions.stem: Both of her parents have normal urinalyses. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in her urine?
options: Increased urinary tryptophan and other neutral amino acids
Increased urinary glucose, phosphate, and bicarbonate
Increased urinary homocystine and methionine
Increased urinary lysine, ornithine, and arginine
approach: Use the pedigree: an affected sibling with unaffected parents fits autosomal recessive inheritance.
Recall the defect: a proximal tubule transporter shared by cystine and the dibasic amino acids.
Predict the urine: cystine plus ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA).
questions.why: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect in a proximal tubule (and intestinal) transporter that carries cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine. All four appear in excess in the urine. Only cystine causes trouble, because it is poorly soluble, especially in acidic urine, and forms hexagonal crystals and stones. The cyanide-nitroprusside test turns positive when urinary cystine is high.
whyNot: Loss of neutral amino acids such as tryptophan is Hartnup disease, which can cause pellagra-like skin findings. It does not cause cystine stones.
Glucose, phosphate, and bicarbonate wasting is Fanconi syndrome, a global proximal tubule failure. Her urine glucose is negative.
Homocystinuria is a defect in methionine metabolism, usually cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. It causes lens dislocation and thrombosis, not kidney stones.
Correct.

dx: Struvite staghorn calculus from Proteus mirabilis infection
case: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of dull left flank pain for 2 months. She has had four urinary tract infections in the past year. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows pH 8.5 (4.5 to 8.0), positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrite, and coffin-lid crystals. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of a gram-negative rod that spreads in waves across the blood agar plate and is identified as Proteus mirabilis. CT scan shows a branching stone that fills the left renal pelvis and calyces. Diagnosis: struvite staghorn calculus due to Proteus mirabilis infection.

questions.stem: Most of the ammonia in her urine comes from bacterial urease. In a healthy person, urinary ammonium comes from the kidney itself. Which of the following best describes this normal renal process?
options: Collecting duct urea hydrolysis that consumes filtered bicarbonate
Distal tubule glycine metabolism that generates titratable acid
Loop of Henle carbonic anhydrase activity that reclaims bicarbonate
Proximal tubule glutamine metabolism that yields new bicarbonate
approach: Separate the two jobs of the kidney in acid-base balance: reclaim filtered bicarbonate and make new bicarbonate.
Recall that new bicarbonate is made when H+ leaves as titratable acid (mainly phosphate) or as ammonium.
Recall the source of ammonium: proximal tubule cells break down glutamine, yielding ammonium for excretion and bicarbonate for the blood.
questions.why: Proximal tubule cells metabolize glutamine into two ammonium ions and two bicarbonate ions. The bicarbonate goes to the blood as new bicarbonate, and the ammonium is secreted and eventually excreted in the urine. Each ammonium excreted represents H+ removed from the body. The kidney does not make urease, so in a healthy person urea passes into the urine intact. In her case, bacterial urease splits urea in the urine itself, producing ammonia that raises urine pH.
whyNot: Human kidneys have no urease. Urea hydrolysis in urine happens only with urease-producing bacteria, as in this patient.
Titratable acid is mostly H+ buffered by filtered phosphate. It is not made by metabolizing glycine.

The thick ascending limb does reclaim some filtered bicarbonate with carbonic anhydrase, and the proximal tubule reclaims most of it. Reclaiming filtered bicarbonate makes no new bicarbonate and no ammonium.
Correct.

questions.stem: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is planned through the posterior flank. After passing through the posterior abdominal wall muscles and transversalis fascia, the access needle traverses which of the following layers, in order, before reaching the renal parenchyma?
options: Perirenal fat, pararenal fat, renal fascia, fibrous capsule
Pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule
Renal fascia, pararenal fat, fibrous capsule, perirenal fat
Pararenal fat, perirenal fat, renal fascia, fibrous capsule
approach: List the coverings from outside in: pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule.
Remember that the renal fascia separates the two fat layers: para (outside) and peri (inside).
The fibrous capsule sticks directly to the kidney surface.
questions.why: The kidney is wrapped in four layers. From outside in, they are the pararenal fat, the renal (Gerota) fascia, the perirenal fat, and the fibrous capsule. The renal fascia encloses the kidney, the perirenal fat, and the suprarenal gland. A posterior approach crosses these layers in that order. The renal fascia also confines perirenal collections, such as a perinephric abscess or hematoma, around the kidney.
whyNot: Perirenal fat lies inside the renal fascia. It cannot be reached before the pararenal fat and the fascia.
Correct.
The pararenal fat lies outside the renal fascia, and the fibrous capsule lies directly on the kidney beneath the perirenal fat.
The two fat layers are separated by the renal fascia, so the needle cannot pass from pararenal fat straight into perirenal fat.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial activities most directly allows the magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals in her stone to form?
options: Acidification of urine by bacterial lactate production
Release of endotoxin that injures the renal papillae
Hydrolysis of urea to ammonia, raising urine pH
Reduction of nitrate to nitrite, chelating urinary magnesium
approach: Name the stone: struvite is magnesium ammonium phosphate.
Recall Proteus urease: it splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Link the result: ammonia raises urine pH and supplies ammonium, and struvite precipitates in alkaline urine.
questions.why: Proteus mirabilis makes large amounts of urease. Urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, and ammonia combines with H+ to form ammonium, raising the urine pH. In alkaline urine, ammonium, magnesium, and phosphate precipitate as struvite, often with carbonate apatite. The stone grows into the calyces as a staghorn, and bacteria live inside it, which keeps the infection going. Proteus also shows swarming motility on agar.
whyNot: Struvite needs alkaline urine. Acidifying the urine would dissolve it.
Endotoxin drives inflammation and sepsis but does not supply the ammonium or the high pH needed for struvite.
Correct.
Nitrate reductase makes the nitrite seen on the dipstick. Nitrite does not chelate magnesium or cause stones.

questions.stem: After nephrolithotomy, she remains hospitalized with an indwelling urinary catheter for 10 days and develops fever. Urine culture grows an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that produces a blue-green pigment and a grape-like odor. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Proteus mirabilis
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
approach: List the clues: oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenter, blue-green pigment, grape-like odor.
Add the setting: a long-term indwelling catheter in a hospitalized patient.
Put them together: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common catheter-associated urinary pathogen.
questions.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. It makes pyocyanin (blue-green) and has a sweet, grape-like odor. It thrives in moist hospital equipment and forms biofilms on catheters, so it is a classic cause of catheter-associated urinary infection. Many strains resist common oral antibiotics.
whyNot: Correct.
Proteus is a non-lactose fermenter but is oxidase negative and shows swarming motility rather than blue-green pigment.
Klebsiella is a lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative rod with a thick mucoid capsule.
Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a gram-positive, novobiocin-resistant coccus that causes cystitis in young sexually active women.

dx: Posterior urethral valves with bilateral hydronephrosis and patent urachus in a newborn boy
case: A male newborn is delivered at 38 weeks' gestation. Prenatal ultrasonography at 30 weeks showed oligohydramnios, bilateral hydronephrosis, and a distended, thick-walled bladder. At birth he has mild respiratory distress. Physical examination shows a palpable suprapubic mass, a weak, dribbling urinary stream, and clear fluid leaking from the umbilicus; the fluid has a creatinine concentration similar to urine. Serum creatinine rises over the first 3 days instead of falling. Voiding cystourethrography shows a dilated posterior urethra with obstructing membranous folds just below the bladder neck. Diagnosis: posterior urethral valves with bilateral hydronephrosis and a patent urachus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his respiratory distress at birth?
options: Surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes
Pulmonary hypoplasia from reduced amniotic fluid
Aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Herniation of bowel through a posterolateral diaphragm defect
approach: Trace the chain: urethral valves block urine outflow from the fetal bladder.
After about 16 weeks, fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid, so blocked outflow causes oligohydramnios.
Too little amniotic fluid limits lung growth, causing pulmonary hypoplasia.
questions.why: Posterior urethral valves are folds of tissue in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of males that block urine outflow. The bladder distends and thickens, and back-pressure dilates both ureters and both kidneys. From the second trimester on, amniotic fluid is mostly fetal urine, so the obstruction causes oligohydramnios. Without enough fluid, the lungs do not develop fully, and the fetus may show the Potter sequence with flat facies and limb deformities.
whyNot: Surfactant deficiency causes respiratory distress in preterm infants. He was born at 38 weeks, and his lungs are small, not immature.
Correct.
Meconium aspiration occurs in post-term or stressed infants. Nothing in this pregnancy points to it.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia also causes lung hypoplasia, but by direct compression. Prenatal imaging here pointed to the urinary tract.

questions.stem: If the obstruction were left untreated for months, which of the following changes would most likely develop in his kidneys?
options: Papillary blunting and thinning of the renal cortex
Bilateral enlargement from many cortical and medullary cysts
Proliferation of parietal epithelium forming glomerular crescents
Nodular mesangial sclerosis with hyaline arteriolosclerosis
approach: Recognize persistent hydronephrosis from outlet obstruction.
Recall the effect of back-pressure: high pressure in the pelvis compresses the papillae and medulla and reduces blood flow.
Predict the lesion: papillary atrophy followed by thinning of the cortex, with a falling GFR.
questions.why: Lasting obstruction raises pressure in the pelvis and calyces. The pressure is transmitted back into the tubules and compresses the renal parenchyma and its blood vessels. The papillae flatten first, then the medulla and cortex thin, and over time the kidney becomes a dilated sac with a thin rim of tissue. GFR falls as nephrons are lost. Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in male infants.
whyNot: Correct.

Massive bilateral enlargement from many cysts is the picture of polycystic kidney disease. Obstruction early in fetal life can cause cystic dysplasia, but continued back-pressure after birth thins the parenchyma instead.
Crescents form in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis from severe glomerular injury, not from back-pressure.
Nodular mesangial sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) with hyaline arteriolosclerosis is diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following embryologic processes failed, leading to the drainage from his umbilicus?
options: Obliteration of the vitelline duct
Obliteration of the distal umbilical arteries
Fusion of the urorectal septum with the cloacal membrane
Obliteration of the allantois
approach: Identify the fluid as urine because its creatinine matches urine.
Find the connection between bladder and umbilicus: the allantois, which becomes the urachus.
Normally the urachus closes into the median umbilical ligament. If it stays open, urine drains from the umbilicus.
questions.why: The allantois extends from the top of the urogenital sinus (the future bladder) into the umbilical cord. Its intra-abdominal part, the urachus, normally closes into a fibrous cord, the median umbilical ligament. If it stays open, urine leaks from the umbilicus. High bladder pressure from outlet obstruction, as with posterior urethral valves, can keep the urachus open. Partial closure leaves a urachal cyst or sinus instead.
whyNot: A patent vitelline duct connects the umbilicus with the ileum and drains intestinal contents, not urine.
The distal umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments. They carry no urine.
Failure of the urorectal septum leaves fistulas between the rectum and the urinary tract. It does not connect the bladder to the umbilicus.
Correct.

questions.stem: Voiding cystourethrography also shows contrast refluxing up both ureters into dilated renal pelves. At 3 weeks of age, he develops fever and Escherichia coli bacteriuria. Which of the following normal defenses has failed most directly?
options: Placental transfer of maternal IgG
Neutrophil adhesion to the bladder urothelium
Flap-valve closure of the intramural ureter
Complement-mediated lysis of gram-negative rods
approach: Link the reflux to the defense: the ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, so bladder pressure normally squeezes it shut.
Explain the failure: high bladder pressure from the valves distorts the ureterovesical junction, so the flap valve no longer closes.
Predict the consequence: infected bladder urine is pushed up to the kidneys.
questions.why: The ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall. When the detrusor contracts, the rising pressure flattens this intramural segment and acts as a one-way flap valve. In posterior urethral valves, chronically high bladder pressure and wall thickening distort this junction, so urine refluxes up the ureters with each void. Reflux carries bacteria to the kidneys and raises the risk of pyelonephritis and scarring.
whyNot: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta normally in a term infant, and antibody levels do not explain urine flowing back up the ureters.
Neutrophil adhesion fails in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, which causes infections without pus and delayed cord separation. It does not cause vesicoureteral reflux.
Correct.
Complement deficiencies predispose to Neisseria and encapsulated organisms. They do not explain reflux of urine into the kidneys.

dx: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction with hydronephrosis in a horseshoe kidney
case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of episodes of dull left flank pain for 6 months. The pain often starts after she drinks large amounts of fluid and resolves within a few hours. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows mild left-sided deep tenderness. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). CT scan shows a horseshoe kidney with its lower poles joined by an isthmus anterior to the aorta at the level of L4. The left renal pelvis and calyces are markedly dilated, with an abrupt narrowing where the pelvis meets the ureter and a normal-caliber ureter below. Diagnosis: ureteropelvic junction obstruction with hydronephrosis in a horseshoe kidney.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures most likely prevented normal ascent of her kidneys during development?
options: Celiac trunk
Superior mesenteric artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
approach: Recall that the metanephric kidneys form in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region between about weeks 6 and 9.
Note that fused lower poles form an isthmus that crosses in front of the aorta.
Identify the vessel that the isthmus catches on during ascent: the inferior mesenteric artery.
questions.why: The permanent kidneys arise in the pelvis and rise toward the lumbar region as the body grows. If the lower poles fuse early, the joined kidney forms a U-shaped horseshoe kidney with an isthmus in front of the aorta. As it rises, the isthmus catches under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidney stays lower than normal, usually at the level of L3 to L5. Horseshoe kidneys carry a higher risk of ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stones, and infection.
whyNot: The celiac trunk arises at about T12, far above the level a horseshoe kidney ever reaches.
The superior mesenteric artery arises at about L1, above the inferior mesenteric artery. The isthmus is caught before it gets that high.
Correct.
The common iliac bifurcation lies at the pelvic brim. The kidneys normally ascend past it, and a horseshoe kidney is caught higher, at the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Two years later, she is pregnant. At 30 weeks' gestation, ultrasonography shows new mild dilation of the right renal pelvis and right ureter down to the pelvic brim, with a normal-caliber ureter below that point. Which of the following best explains this new finding?
options: Progression of her congenital ureteropelvic junction narrowing
A ureteral stone impacted at the ureterovesical junction
Vesicoureteral reflux through an incompetent ureterovesical junction
Compression of the ureter by the enlarged uterus at the pelvic brim
approach: Find the level: the ureter is dilated only above the pelvic brim.
Match the level to a cause: in late pregnancy the uterus compresses the ureter where it crosses the pelvic brim, more often on the right.
Exclude the others by side or level: her known narrowing is on the left, and a distal stone or reflux would dilate the whole ureter.
questions.why: Hydronephrosis has typical causes by age and sex. Infants and children have ureteropelvic junction obstruction and posterior urethral valves; young adults have stones; pregnant women have compression by the uterus; older men have prostatic enlargement; and older women have pelvic tumors such as cervical cancer. In pregnancy the enlarged uterus presses on the ureter at the pelvic brim, and progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle. The right side is affected more often because the uterus usually rotates to the right.
whyNot: Her ureteropelvic junction narrowing is on the left, and it dilates only the pelvis and calyces, not the ureter.
A stone at the ureterovesical junction would dilate the ureter all the way down to the bladder.
Reflux dilates the full length of the ureter from the bladder upward, not only the part above the pelvic brim.
Correct.

topics: Causes of hydronephrosis by age and sex

questions.stem: After delivery, she develops fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), left flank pain, and Escherichia coli bacteriuria. Voiding cystourethrography shows no reflux, and the left renal pelvis remains dilated. Which of the following best explains why the left kidney is more prone to infection than the right?
options: Stagnant urine that is not cleared by antegrade flow
Loss of Tamm-Horsfall protein secretion by the left kidney
Reduced shedding of urothelial cells in the renal pelvis
Bacterial entry through a defective ureterovesical flap valve
approach: Note the asymmetry: only the left side has a dilated, poorly draining pelvis.
Recall the most important defense: steady one-way flow of urine washes bacteria out.
Apply it: stagnant urine in the obstructed pelvis lets bacteria multiply.
questions.why: The urinary tract is protected mostly by flow. Urine moves steadily from kidney to bladder and is emptied completely, which flushes bacteria out before they can multiply. Above an obstruction, urine pools in a dilated pelvis and turns over slowly, giving bacteria time to grow. Obstruction anywhere in the tract therefore raises the risk of pyelonephritis on that side.
whyNot: Correct.
Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) is made by the thick ascending limb of both kidneys and binds bacteria. There is no reason for it to be lost on one side.
Urothelial shedding helps clear attached bacteria, but obstruction does not selectively stop it. Stasis is the main problem.
The study showed no reflux, so the ureterovesical flap valve is working.

questions.stem: A pyeloplasty is performed. In a normally positioned left kidney, which of the following structures lies directly anterior to the renal hilum?
options: Second part of the duodenum
Tail of the pancreas
Hepatic flexure of the colon
Visceral surface of the liver
approach: Work out the side: this question is about the left kidney.
List the anterior relations of the left kidney: stomach, spleen, tail of the pancreas, jejunum, and the left colic flexure.
Choose the structure at the hilum: the pancreatic tail lies across it.
questions.why: The left kidney is related anteriorly to the stomach above, the spleen laterally, the tail of the pancreas across the hilum, the jejunum below and medially, and the left colic flexure and descending colon laterally. The right kidney is related to the liver, the descending (second) part of the duodenum near its hilum, and the right colic (hepatic) flexure. These relations matter in trauma and surgery near either kidney.
whyNot: The second part of the duodenum lies in front of the hilum of the right kidney.
Correct.
The hepatic (right colic) flexure lies in front of the lower pole of the right kidney.
The liver lies in front of the upper part of the right kidney.

dx: Ureteral ligation with hydronephrosis after hysterectomy
case: A 46-year-old woman has right flank pain 4 days after an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine leiomyomas. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Her urine output is normal. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), unchanged from before surgery. Ultrasonography shows moderate right hydronephrosis and a dilated right ureter; the left kidney is normal. CT urography shows that contrast in the right ureter stops abruptly in the distal ureter, with no leakage. At repeat operation, a suture is found around the right ureter. Diagnosis: inadvertent ligation of the right ureter during hysterectomy, with hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: Immediately after the ligation, which of the following changes most directly reduced the glomerular filtration rate of the right kidney?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space
Increased oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
Decreased hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
Decreased oncotic pressure in Bowman space
approach: Write the Starling balance: GFR depends on capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space hydrostatic pressure minus capillary oncotic pressure.
Ask which term the blockage changes: urine backs up from the ureter into the tubules and Bowman space.
Raised Bowman space pressure opposes filtration, so GFR falls.
questions.why: Net filtration pressure equals glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space hydrostatic pressure minus glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (Bowman space oncotic pressure is near zero). A blocked ureter raises pressure in the pelvis, tubules, and Bowman space, which pushes against filtration. Hypoalbuminemia does the opposite by lowering capillary oncotic pressure, and dehydration lowers GFR mainly by reducing renal blood flow and capillary pressure.
whyNot: Correct.
Capillary oncotic pressure rises with dehydration or when filtration fraction increases. A ureteral ligature does not change plasma proteins.
Glomerular capillary pressure falls with afferent arteriolar constriction or low blood pressure, as in prerenal states. The ligature acts downstream of the glomerulus.
Bowman space oncotic pressure is already close to zero. A fall would favor filtration, not reduce it.

questions.stem: Years later, she is the restrained driver in a motor vehicle collision while her bladder is full. CT cystography shows contrast outlining loops of small bowel. Which of the following best explains the location of the contrast?
options: Rupture of the bladder neck below the peritoneal reflection
Rupture of the peritoneum-covered bladder dome
Rupture of the anterior wall into the retropubic space
Rupture of the pelvic ureter at the iliac vessels
approach: Read the image: contrast around bowel loops means it is inside the peritoneal cavity.
Recall the bladder's relation to peritoneum: only the dome (superior surface) is covered by peritoneum.
A sudden blow to a full bladder bursts the dome, its weakest part, and urine spills into the peritoneal cavity.
questions.why: The kidneys and ureters lie behind the peritoneum, and the bladder lies below it, with peritoneum covering only its superior surface (the dome). When a full bladder is struck, pressure spikes and the dome ruptures, so urine leaks into the peritoneal cavity. Pelvic fractures more often tear the bladder near its neck or anterior wall, and urine then leaks into the extraperitoneal tissues around the bladder.
whyNot: Rupture of the bladder neck occurs below the peritoneum, so contrast collects in the extraperitoneal pelvic tissues.
Correct.
Anterior wall tears, often from pelvic fracture fragments, leak into the retropubic space, which lies outside the peritoneum.
The ureter is retroperitoneal. A ureteral tear leaks into the retroperitoneum, not around bowel loops.

topics: Peritoneal relations of the urinary tract

questions.stem: At which of the following sites was the ureter most likely ligated during the hysterectomy?
options: At the ureteropelvic junction near the renal hilum
At the pelvic brim anterior to the iliac vessels
Lateral to the cervix beneath the uterine artery
Within the bladder wall at the ureteral orifice
approach: Recall the step of hysterectomy where the ureter is most at risk: clamping and tying the uterine artery.
Recall the anatomy: in the base of the broad ligament, about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, the uterine artery passes over the ureter.
A suture placed around the artery here can catch the ureter.
questions.why: In the base of the broad ligament, the uterine artery crosses above and in front of the ureter about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, a relation often remembered as water under the bridge. When the uterine vessels are clamped and tied, the ureter can be caught in the ligature or cut. Ligation causes hydronephrosis above the tie, while transection causes a urine leak and urinoma or a fistula.
whyNot: The ureteropelvic junction lies near the kidney, far from the operative field of a hysterectomy.
The ureter does cross the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, but this site is above the uterine vessels and is not where the uterine artery is tied.
Correct.
The intramural ureter lies within the bladder wall. Injury there would come from bladder surgery, and it is not the classic site in hysterectomy.

questions.stem: Her serum creatinine remained normal despite complete obstruction of the right ureter. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Tubular secretion of creatinine by the obstructed right kidney
Lower creatinine generation from postoperative muscle loss
Dilution of serum creatinine by intravenous fluids
Adequate filtration by the unobstructed left kidney
approach: Note that only one ureter is blocked.
Recall that one healthy kidney can clear enough creatinine to keep serum creatinine near normal.
Contrast with bilateral obstruction (or obstruction of a single kidney), which causes postrenal acute kidney injury.
questions.why: Unilateral obstruction often causes few signs beyond flank pain, because the other kidney compensates. Serum creatinine and urine output stay near normal, and the problem can be missed until imaging shows hydronephrosis. Postrenal acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria requires obstruction of both kidneys, of a single functioning kidney, or of the bladder outlet.
whyNot: Secretion into a tubule that cannot drain does not remove creatinine from the body. The blocked kidney contributes little clearance.
Creatinine production falls only slowly with muscle loss and would not mask the loss of a kidney's function after a few days.
Intravenous fluids lower serum creatinine only slightly and briefly. They do not explain a stable value over several days.
Correct.

dx: Postrenal acute kidney injury from benign prostatic hyperplasia with postobstructive diuresis
case: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has passed only small amounts of urine for 3 days. He has had nocturia, hesitancy, and a weak stream for several years. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg. The bladder is palpable to the umbilicus. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery prostate. Serum studies show urea nitrogen (BUN) 68 mg/dL (7 to 20), creatinine 4.2 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), potassium 6.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (22 to 28). Ultrasonography shows bilateral hydronephrosis. A urethral catheter drains 1600 mL. Over the next 24 hours, his urine output is about 400 mL/h. Diagnosis: postrenal acute kidney injury from benign prostatic hyperplasia, with postobstructive diuresis.

questions.stem: An ECG shows peaked T waves. He is given intravenous insulin with glucose, and his serum potassium falls within 30 minutes. Which of the following best explains this effect?
options: Increased potassium secretion by collecting duct principal cells
Increased potassium loss through colonic epithelium
Stabilization of cardiac membranes against potassium
Stimulation of Na+/K+-ATPase in muscle and liver cells
approach: Note the speed: a fall within 30 minutes means a shift into cells, not removal from the body.
Recall what insulin does to potassium: it activates the Na+/K+-ATPase, mainly in skeletal muscle and liver.
Conclude that potassium moves from the blood into cells while total body potassium stays the same.
questions.why: Insulin activates the Na+/K+-ATPase, which pumps potassium into cells. Beta-2 agonists and alkalosis also shift potassium inward. Acidosis, cell lysis, insulin deficiency, and hyperosmolality shift it out, and his metabolic acidosis adds to his hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves and, when severe, a wide QRS. A shift buys time, but the potassium still has to be removed from the body, here by relieving the obstruction.
whyNot: Aldosterone, not insulin, is the main driver of potassium secretion by principal cells, and that effect takes hours.
The colon secretes some potassium, and binding resins work there, but insulin does not act this way.
Calcium, not insulin, stabilizes the cardiac membrane. It protects the heart without lowering serum potassium.
Correct.

questions.stem: He requires an indwelling urethral catheter for 2 weeks while awaiting surgery. Which of the following best explains why the catheter raises his risk of urinary tract infection?
options: It suppresses neutrophil migration into the bladder wall
It neutralizes the acidity of the urine within the bladder
It lets bacteria ascend in a biofilm along its surface
It blocks secretion of IgA by the urothelium
approach: List the normal defenses: a closed urethra, regular flushing by voiding, and a urothelium that sheds attached bacteria.
Ask what a catheter does: it holds the urethra open and gives bacteria a surface to grow on.
Conclude that bacteria climb along the catheter in a biofilm that the defenses cannot reach.
questions.why: A catheter bypasses the urethral sphincter and the flushing action of voiding. Bacteria from the perineum or the drainage system attach to the catheter surface and form a biofilm that protects them from antibodies, neutrophils, and many antibiotics. They then climb along the outside or inside of the catheter into the bladder. The risk rises each day the catheter stays in place, which is why catheters are removed as soon as possible.
whyNot: Catheters do not suppress neutrophil function. Neutrophils still enter the bladder wall, but they cannot clear bacteria inside a biofilm.
Urine pH is not the main defense, and catheters do not neutralize urine acidity.
Correct.
Secretory IgA plays only a small role in the bladder, and a catheter does not block its secretion.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his large urine output after the catheter is placed?
options: Glucose-driven osmotic diuresis after insulin treatment
Urea diuresis plus impaired tubular concentrating ability
Central suppression of ADH release after bladder decompression
Afferent arteriolar dilation that raises glomerular filtration
approach: Recognize postobstructive diuresis after relief of bilateral obstruction.
Identify the retained solute: urea and sodium built up while both kidneys were blocked, and they are now filtered and excreted.
Add the tubular injury: back-pressure damaged the tubules and washed out the medullary gradient, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine.
questions.why: Bilateral obstruction (here at the bladder outlet) causes postrenal acute kidney injury. Unilateral obstruction usually does not, because the other kidney compensates. After relief, the kidneys excrete the urea, sodium, and water retained during the obstruction. Back-pressure has also injured the tubules, reduced the medullary concentration gradient, and blunted the response to ADH, so the urine is dilute and large in volume. Severe diuresis can cause volume depletion and electrolyte losses.
whyNot: His glucose was given with insulin and would not reach levels high enough to cause glucosuria and osmotic diuresis.
Correct.
Draining the bladder does not suppress ADH release. The problem lies in the kidney's response to ADH, not in its secretion.
Relief of obstruction lowers Bowman space pressure, but this restores filtration toward normal. It does not explain urine output far above normal.

questions.stem: Before catheterization, he had constant dribbling of small volumes from a large bladder. A similar overflow pattern without any outlet obstruction is most likely to result from which of the following lesions?
options: Destruction of the sacral cord segments S2 to S4
Complete transection of the spinal cord at the T6 level
Infarction of the medial frontal cortex above the pons
Demyelinating plaque in the cervical spinal cord
approach: Identify the bladder type: large, overfilled, and dribbling means a flaccid overflow bladder.
Recall the reflex: detrusor contraction depends on parasympathetic efferents in the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4.
A lesion that destroys the sacral reflex center leaves the detrusor unable to contract.
questions.why: Micturition is a spinal reflex at S2 to S4 that is coordinated by the pontine micturition center and controlled by the frontal cortex. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves contract the detrusor, sympathetic fibers from about T11 to L2 relax it and close the internal sphincter, and the pudendal nerve controls the external sphincter. Damage at the sacral cord or cauda equina abolishes the reflex, so the bladder fills until it overflows. Lesions above the sacral cord leave the reflex intact but uncoordinated, giving a small, spastic bladder.
whyNot: Correct.
A T6 transection spares the sacral reflex arc but cuts pontine control. After spinal shock, the bladder becomes small and spastic and empties reflexly.
A frontal lesion removes cortical inhibition, causing urgency and uninhibited voiding of normal or small volumes.
A cervical plaque in multiple sclerosis is above the sacral cord and causes a spastic bladder, often with detrusor and sphincter dyssynergia.

dx: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis from a proton pump inhibitor
case: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, low-grade fever, and a rash for 5 days. She started omeprazole for gastroesophageal reflux 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. A maculopapular rash covers her trunk. Serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1); 2 months ago it was 0.9 mg/dL. Leukocyte count is 9800/mm3 with 9% eosinophils (1 to 4). Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, trace protein, 20 to 30 WBCs/hpf, and WBC casts. Urine culture shows no growth. Diagnosis: acute interstitial nephritis caused by omeprazole.

questions.stem: Which of the following best interprets her urinalysis?
options: Bacterial cystitis with nitrate-reducing gram-negative rods
Sterile pyuria arising from inflammation within the kidney
Contamination of the specimen by vaginal leukocytes
Lower urinary tract inflammation from urethritis
approach: Read each result: leukocyte esterase means pyuria; a negative nitrite and a negative culture mean no usual bacterial infection.
Localize the source: WBC casts form only inside renal tubules.
Conclude that this is sterile pyuria from inflammation in the kidney.
questions.why: Leukocyte esterase detects white cells in the urine. Nitrite appears when Enterobacterales such as Escherichia coli reduce dietary nitrate, so a negative nitrite with a sterile culture argues against a common bacterial infection. Casts are molded in the tubules, so WBC casts place the inflammation in the kidney, as in interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis. Sterile pyuria without casts suggests urethritis, as from Chlamydia, or renal tuberculosis.
whyNot: Bacterial cystitis would usually give a positive nitrite and a positive culture, and it would not produce WBC casts.
Correct.
Contamination brings squamous cells and leukocytes but cannot produce casts, which form only in renal tubules.
Urethritis causes sterile pyuria, but the inflammation is below the kidney, so there would be no WBC casts.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy shows interstitial edema with an infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils invading the tubules; the glomeruli are normal. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for her kidney injury?
options: Immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Antibodies against type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane
Direct dose-dependent toxicity to proximal tubular cells
Delayed hypersensitivity to a drug-modified tubular antigen
approach: Note the timing and systemic signs: fever, rash, and eosinophilia beginning weeks after a new drug.
Read the biopsy: interstitial inflammation with eosinophils and tubulitis, but normal glomeruli.
Conclude that this is an immune hypersensitivity reaction to the drug in the interstitium, mainly T cell mediated.
questions.why: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis is an immune reaction, not a toxic one. The drug or its metabolite binds to tubular or interstitial proteins and acts as a hapten, and T cells react against the new antigen (a delayed, type IV reaction), often with features of IgE-mediated hypersensitivity such as eosinophilia. It begins days to weeks after starting drugs such as penicillins, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, and diuretics, and it does not depend on the dose. Stopping the drug usually leads to recovery.
whyNot: Immune complex deposition causes glomerulonephritis with granular deposits. Her glomeruli are normal.
Anti-type IV collagen antibodies cause anti-GBM disease with crescents and linear IgG staining, and often lung hemorrhage.
Direct dose-dependent toxicity, as with aminoglycosides, causes acute tubular necrosis without fever, rash, or eosinophilia.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her BUN is 34 mg/dL (7 to 20), fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is 2.6 percent, and urine osmolality is 320 mOsm/kg H2O. Volume depletion from poor oral intake had been suspected at first. Which of the following sets of findings would have supported volume depletion as the cause of her rising creatinine?
options: BUN to creatinine ratio above 20, FENa below 1 percent, urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg
BUN to creatinine ratio below 15, FENa above 2 percent, urine osmolality below 350 mOsm/kg
BUN to creatinine ratio above 20, FENa above 2 percent, urine osmolality below 350 mOsm/kg
BUN to creatinine ratio below 15, FENa below 1 percent, urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg
approach: Recall that in prerenal injury the tubules work normally and hold on to sodium, water, and urea.
Predict the indices: FENa under 1 percent, concentrated urine above 500 mOsm/kg, and a BUN to creatinine ratio over 20 because urea is reabsorbed with water.
Compare her values: a ratio of about 13, FENa 2.6 percent, and dilute urine point to intrinsic injury.
questions.why: Acute kidney injury is classified as prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal. In prerenal states, low perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH, so the healthy tubules keep sodium and water, and urea follows water back into the blood. This gives a FENa below 1 percent, a high urine osmolality, and a BUN to creatinine ratio above 20. In intrinsic disease such as acute tubular necrosis or interstitial nephritis, damaged tubules lose sodium and cannot concentrate urine, giving a FENa above 2 percent and urine osmolality near plasma.
whyNot: Correct.
This set fits intrinsic tubular injury, which matches her actual values, not volume depletion.
A high ratio with a high FENa and dilute urine is a mixed pattern that does not fit healthy tubules responding to low perfusion.
A low FENa with concentrated urine suggests intact tubules, but a ratio below 15 argues against the extra urea reabsorption of a prerenal state.

topics: FENa and BUN to creatinine ratio

questions.stem: Two weeks after the drug is stopped, her serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. Serum studies show sodium 138 mEq/L (136 to 145), potassium 5.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), chloride 112 mEq/L (98 to 106), and bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (22 to 28). Urine pH is 5.0. Which of the following best describes her acid-base disorder?
options: Distal (type 1) RTA with impaired H+ secretion
Proximal (type 2) RTA with bicarbonate wasting
Type 4 RTA from reduced aldosterone effect
Anion gap acidosis from uremic acid retention
approach: Calculate the anion gap: 138 minus 112 minus 18 equals 8, which is normal.
Use potassium to sort the RTAs: hyperkalemia points to type 4, while types 1 and 2 cause hypokalemia.
Check the urine pH: it is below 5.5, which fits type 4 and rules out type 1.
questions.why: Type 4 RTA comes from low aldosterone or from tubules that do not respond to it, which is common in tubulointerstitial disease. Without aldosterone action, principal cells secrete less potassium and intercalated cells secrete less H+. The hyperkalemia also suppresses ammonium production from glutamine in the proximal tubule, so the kidney excretes less acid. The result is a normal anion gap acidosis with hyperkalemia, and the urine can still be acidified below 5.5.
whyNot: Distal RTA causes hypokalemia and a urine pH above 5.5 despite acidemia.
Proximal RTA causes hypokalemia from bicarbonate and sodium delivery to the distal nephron.
Correct.
Retained uremic anions widen the anion gap, mostly when GFR is much lower. Her anion gap is normal.

case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of left flank pain and red urine for 1 day. She passed a small piece of tissue in her urine this morning. She has taken daily combination analgesic tablets containing aspirin, acetaminophen, and caffeine for chronic headaches for 20 years. She has never smoked. Vital signs are within normal limits. Serum creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Urinalysis shows many RBCs, 10 to 15 WBCs/hpf, and no bacteria; urine culture shows no growth. CT scan shows small kidneys with irregular contours and calcified renal papillae. Diagnosis: analgesic nephropathy with chronic interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions also predisposes to the papillary lesion seen in this patient?
options: Minimal change disease in a child
Membranous nephropathy with nephrotic syndrome
Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
approach: Name the lesion: papillary necrosis, ischemic death of the tips of the medullary pyramids.
List its causes: analgesics, diabetes, sickle cell disease, severe pyelonephritis, and obstruction.
Pick the option on that list.
questions.why: Papillary necrosis is ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae. Its classic causes are long-term combination analgesic use, diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease or trait, severe acute pyelonephritis, and urinary obstruction. Diabetes contributes through small-vessel disease and a higher risk of infection. A sloughed papilla can block the ureter and cause colic and hematuria, as in this patient.
whyNot: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with podocyte foot process effacement and spares the papillae.
Membranous nephropathy is an immune complex disease of the glomerular basement membrane. It does not cause papillary necrosis.
Correct.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex glomerular disease that causes the nephritic syndrome, not papillary necrosis.

questions.stem: Long-term aspirin use inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and reduces vasodilation in the renal medulla. Which of the following best explains why the papillae are more vulnerable to this effect than the cortex?
options: Slow vasa recta flow keeps papillary oxygen tension low
Juxtamedullary glomeruli receive most of the renal blood flow
Cortical peritubular capillaries supply the papillae
Papillary cells rely mainly on oxidative fatty acid metabolism
approach: Recall the medullary blood supply: the vasa recta, which carry only a small share of renal blood flow.
Recall the countercurrent arrangement: slow flow and oxygen diffusion from descending to ascending vessels keep oxygen tension at the papillary tip low.
Apply it: tissue that is already near hypoxia dies first when prostaglandin-driven vasodilation is lost.
questions.why: The medulla receives only a small share of renal blood flow, carried by the vasa recta. Their slow flow and hairpin, countercurrent arrangement preserve medullary hypertonicity by keeping solute from being washed out. The same arrangement lets oxygen diffuse from descending to ascending vessels, so the papillary tip has a very low oxygen tension. Prostaglandins help keep medullary flow up, so blocking them can tip the papillae into ischemic necrosis. Low oxygen tension also explains why red cells sickle in the vasa recta.
whyNot: Correct.
Most renal blood flow goes to the cortex, not to the juxtamedullary glomeruli or the medulla.
The papillae are supplied by the vasa recta, which come from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, not by cortical peritubular capillaries.
Medullary cells depend more on anaerobic glycolysis because oxygen there is scarce, not on oxidative fatty acid metabolism.

questions.stem: Five years later, she has painless gross hematuria. CT urography shows a papillary filling defect within the left renal pelvis, and the renal parenchyma is not expanded. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
Angiomyolipoma
Oncocytoma
Urothelial carcinoma
approach: Locate the mass: it arises from the lining of the renal pelvis, not from the renal parenchyma.
Recall the tumor of that lining: urothelial carcinoma.
Link the risk factor: long-term analgesic use, especially phenacetin-containing mixtures, raises the risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
questions.why: The renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder are lined by urothelium, and urothelial carcinoma is the main tumor of that lining. It usually presents with painless hematuria and tends to be multifocal and to recur. Major risk factors are smoking, aromatic amine dyes, cyclophosphamide, and long-term analgesic use with phenacetin. Patients with analgesic nephropathy have a clearly increased risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
whyNot: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma arises from proximal tubule cells in the cortex and expands the renal parenchyma.
Angiomyolipoma is a parenchymal tumor of vessels, smooth muscle, and fat, linked to tuberous sclerosis.
Oncocytoma is a benign parenchymal tumor from intercalated cells, with a central scar on imaging.
Correct.

questions.stem: Years before her flank pain began, she had nocturia, and her urine osmolality stayed close to that of plasma. Loss of which of the following nephron populations most directly impairs urine concentration?
options: Cortical nephrons with short loops of Henle and peritubular capillaries
Juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops and vasa recta
Cortical nephrons with long loops and vasa recta
Juxtamedullary nephrons with short loops and peritubular capillaries
approach: Note the early sign: a concentrating defect, which reflects medullary and papillary injury.
Recall the two nephron types: juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli near the medulla, long loops reaching the papilla, and vasa recta.
Conclude that loss of the long loops removes the deep medullary gradient needed to concentrate urine.
questions.why: Cortical nephrons make up most nephrons. Their glomeruli lie in the outer cortex, their loops of Henle are short, and their tubules are surrounded by peritubular capillaries. Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction, long loops that reach deep into the papilla, and efferent arterioles that form the vasa recta. Their long loops build the steep medullary gradient that lets ADH concentrate urine. Papillary damage destroys these loops early, causing nocturia and urine that cannot be concentrated.
whyNot: Cortical nephrons do have short loops and peritubular capillaries, but they add little to the deep medullary gradient, and they are spared early in papillary disease.
Correct.
Cortical nephrons have short loops and peritubular capillaries, not long loops and vasa recta.
Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and vasa recta, not short loops and peritubular capillaries.
